messages.subject: misspecifying multivariate multilevel negative binomial model
parts:
I am working on a multivariate multilevel negative binomial model in pyStan. However, the model fails without me explicitly setting one of my parameters, and this is wrong. I generated fake data that represents two groups of predators eating two groups of prey with the following code. The idea as that there is increased consumption of each prey group at higher temperatures, and later in the day, prey have accumulated in the guts.

import numpy as np
import pystan

# fake dat
N = 250 # number per groups (must be factor of ten)

# array of temperatures
base_temp = 25
# temperature for group 1
temp_1 = np.random.normal(base_temp, 0.1, N)
# temperature for group 2
temp_2 = np.random.normal(base_temp + 2, 0.1, N)
temp = np.append(temp_1, temp_2)

# array of hours past sunrise (10 per day)
hours = np.repeat(np.arange(0, 10), N / 5)

prob_param = temp * 0.02 + hours * -0.04

prey_1 = np.empty(N * 2)
prey_2 = np.empty(N * 2)

for i in range(0, N * 2):
    # number of prey for each member of group 1
    prey_1[i] = np.random.negative_binomial(1, prob_param[i] + 0.07, 1)
    # number of prey for each member of group 2
    prey_2[i] = np.random.negative_binomial(1, prob_param[i], 1)

group = np.append(np.ones(N), np.ones(N) + 1).astype(int)

y = np.matrix([list(prey_1), list(prey_2)]).T
x = np.matrix([list(temp), list(hours)]).T

model_dat = ({'N':len(y),
             'X': np.shape(x)[1],
             'Y': np.shape(y)[1],
             'L': len(np.unique(group)),
             'y': y.astype(int),
             'x': x,
             'random': group,
             })

Finally I set up my model and run in Python as follows:

model_code = """
    data {
      int<lower=0> N; //rows of data
      int<lower=1> X; // number of covariates
      int<lower=1> Y; // number of responses
      int<lower=1> L; // number of groups
      vector[X] x[N]; // design matrix (predictors)
      int<lower=0> y[N,Y]; // response (outcomes)
      int<lower=1, upper=L> random[N]; // groups
    }
    parameters {
      vector[Y] intercept; // Population intercept
      matrix[Y,X] beta; // Population slope parameters
      cholesky_factor_corr[Y] omega;
      cholesky_factor_corr[L] omega_u;
      vector<lower=0>[Y] sigma; // population standard deviation
      vector[L] u; // random effects
      vector<lower=0>[L] sigma_u; // random effects SD
    }
    transformed parameters {
      matrix[L,Y] mu;
      vector[L] beta_0j; // varying intercepts
      // negative binomial beta parameter for each group and response
      matrix<lower=0>[L,Y] NB_beta;
      // negative binomial alpha parameter for each group and response
      matrix<lower=0>[L,Y] alpha;
      
      //Varying intercepts definition
      beta_0j <- intercept + u;
      
      for (i in 1:Y) { // for each response variable
        for (l in 1:L) { // for each group
          mu[,l] <- beta * x[i,] + beta_0j[random[l]];
          NB_beta[,l]<-exp(mu[,l]); // log link
          }
        }
    }
    model {
      matrix[Y,Y] Sigma;
      matrix[L,L] Sigma_u;
      vector[L] zeros;
      
      to_vector(beta) ~ normal(0, 2);
      
      Sigma <- diag_pre_multiply(sigma, omega);
      Sigma_u <- diag_pre_multiply(sigma_u, omega_u);
      
      zeros <- rep_vector(0, L);
      
      // Priors
      u ~ multi_normal_cholesky(zeros, Sigma_u);
      intercept ~ multi_normal_cholesky(zeros, Sigma);
      omega ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(4);
      omega_u ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(4);
      sigma ~ normal(0,2);
      sigma_u ~ normal(0,2);
    
      // Data Model
      for (i in 1:N) // for each predator
        y[i] ~ neg_binomial(alpha[random[i]], NB_beta[random[i]]);
    }
    """

fit = pystan.stan(model_code=model_code, data=model_dat,
                  iter=1000, chains=2,
                  model_name='diet',
                  sample_file='/Users/username/Desktop/sample')

Sorry the lowercase "l" looks so much like the numeral 1 here. The code will compile, but when I do its starts by telling me:

Rejecting initial value:
  Error evaluating the log probability at the initial value.

and after a bunch of warnings the last bit of the output looks like:

Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:
validate transformed params: alpha[1] is nan, but must be greater than or equal to 0
If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,
but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified.

Rejecting initial value:
  Error evaluating the log probability at the initial value.

Initialization between (--2, -2) failed after 100 attempts. 
 Try specifying initial values, reducing ranges of constrained values, or reparameterizing the model.

I think this is probably just a terribly specified model, but it is interesting that adding alpha <- rep_vector(1, L) to the transformed parameters block will actually allow it to run, although one of the NB_Beta values is ridiculously high. I'm hoping I'm missing a key prior or something. Does anyone see any glaring problems with the model, or have any other suggestions to improve the code? Thanks.

Jason

Right --- you have to define variables in the transformed
parameters block before using them. The only two kinds of
variable you don't have to define before using are those
defined in the data and parameters blocks.

- Bob

parts:
Thanks very much. The reason I had it in the transformed block was so that I could see the parameter values of alpha in the table output. I will work on incorporating your suggestions. Knowing that alpha is close to one for my data, I tested the fit of the model anyway (with alpha hard-coded to 1), and I am quite surprised by the goodness the fit. One thing I notice in that the output NB_beta parameters don't seem to vary between the 2 prey types. So there is still something wrong with the model structure it seems. Still I am happy with my progress so far. Anyway, if any of you are Python users, this is the code I used to view the negative binomial fits to my fake data. Blue represents the actual data, red represents the predictions (plotted as a line for simplicity in viewing). 

# it might help to give you Gelman's negative binomial function!

from scipy.special import binom

def Gelman_NB(theta, alpha, beta):
    term1 = binom((theta + alpha - 1),(alpha - 1))
    term2 = (beta / (beta + 1)) ** alpha
    term3 = (1 / (beta + 1)) ** theta
    x = term1 * term2 * term3
    return x

prey_id = [1,2]
prey = [prey_1, prey_2]
beta = [np.nan, 0.80, 0.39] // taken from output table of fit parameters, there are actually 4 for NB_beta, but 2 each are the same, so I simplified things here
for i in range(0,2):
    for j in range(1,3):
        a = Gelman_NB(np.arange(0,10), 1.0, beta[j]) * 250
        plt.plot(np.arange(0,10) + 0.5, a, color='red')
        binned = np.histogram(prey[i][group==j], np.arange(0,10))
        plt.bar(np.arange(0,9), binned[0])
        print('group = ' + str(j) + ' prey = ' + str(i + 1))
        plt.show()

parts:
You need to *define* values before using them in Stan.

real x; // declared, but not defined
x ~ normal(0, 1); // BAD, crashes with NaN

real x;
x <- alpha + beta * 3;
x ~ normal(0, 1); // OK, assuming alpha and beta are defined

The only time you don't need to define a variable is if it's
declared in the data or parameters block.

- Bob

parts: Both have you have given me great advice, and hopefully gotten me one step closer to a working model. Although, I'm still not sure how I can output the alpha and beta parameters without putting it in the transformed parameters section. Setting my alpha parameter has done the trick, and the output table looks like I think it should. Its probably not very efficient how it is coded at the moment. But I worry more about getting it right than efficient. Still, something doesn't feel right. For one thing, the data and predicted distributions aren't in great agreement, but in the right ballpark I guess (not as good as when I forced alpha to 1). I also kind of feel like I'm doing multiple univariate regressions rather than a true multivariate model, but hopefully I'm wrong about this. Anyway this is how I specified my model. It seemed the clear way to specify alpha was NB_beta * mu, based on Gelman's NB formulation.

model_code = """
    data {
      int<lower=0> N; //rows of data
      int<lower=1> X; // number of covariates
      int<lower=1> Y; // number of responses
      int<lower=1> L; // number of groups
      vector[X] x[N]; // design matrix (predictors)
      int<lower=0> y[N,Y]; // response (outcomes)
      int<lower=1, upper=L> random[N];
    }

parameters {
      vector[Y] intercept; // Population intercept
      matrix[Y,X] beta; // Population slope parameters
      cholesky_factor_corr[Y] omega;
      cholesky_factor_corr[L] omega_u;
      vector<lower=0>[Y] sigma; // population standard deviation
vector[L] u; // random intercepts

vector<lower=0>[L] sigma_u; // random effects SD
    }
    transformed parameters {
// matrices are column-major, y has N-rows

matrix[L,Y] mu;
      vector[L] beta_0j; // varying intercepts
      // negative binomial beta parameter for each group and response
      matrix<lower=0>[L,Y] NB_beta;
      // negative binomial alpha parameter for each group and response
      matrix<lower=0>[L,Y] alpha;
      
      //Varying intercepts definition
      beta_0j <- intercept + u;
// each response may have different slopes and intercepts
for (i in 1:Y) { // for each response
for (l in 1:L) { // for each group

for (j in 1:X) { // for each covariate
            for (n in 1:N) { // for each individual
              mu[l,i] <- beta[l,i] * x[n,j] + intercept[i] + beta_0j[random[l]];
              }
            }
          NB_beta[l,i]<-exp(mu[l,i]); // log link
          alpha[l,i] <- NB_beta[l,i] * mu[l,i];

}
        }
    }
    model {
      matrix[Y,Y] Sigma;
      matrix[L,L] Sigma_u;
      vector[L] zeros;
      
      to_vector(beta) ~ normal(0, 2);
      
      Sigma <- diag_pre_multiply(sigma, omega);
      Sigma_u <- diag_pre_multiply(sigma_u, omega_u);
      
      zeros <- rep_vector(0, L);
      
      // Priors
      u ~ multi_normal_cholesky(zeros, Sigma_u);
      intercept ~ multi_normal_cholesky(zeros, Sigma);
      omega ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(4);
      omega_u ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(4);
      sigma ~ normal(0,2);
      sigma_u ~ normal(0,2);
for (i in 1:Y) { // for each response
for (l in 1:L) { // for each group

alpha[l,i] ~ gamma(5,1);
          NB_beta[l,i] ~ gamma(2,2);
        }
      }
    
      // Data Model
      for (i in 1:N) // for each individual

y[i] ~ neg_binomial(alpha[random[i]], NB_beta[random[i]]);
    }
    """

binned = np.histogram(prey[i][group == j + 1], np.arange(0,10))
